Session‑based recommendation (SBR) seeks to predict the next item a user will click based solely on the short, anonymous interaction sequence within a single visit.  The seminal SR‑GNN model introduced the idea of converting each session into a directed item‑transition graph and applying a gated graph neural network to learn item embeddings that capture complex, non‑sequential dependencies, thereby outperforming traditional RNN‑based approaches [S2:0c7e1338a9c7914a3b9a5bdc42b457b3f272160e].  Shortly thereafter, NISER highlighted that raw graph propagation can be biased by item popularity and proposed normalized item and session representations to obtain more balanced embeddings [S2:65b8145199089d484a4d9e0baeb2e1ce9145d6fd].  Parallel work on graph‑based collaborative filtering demonstrated that embedding users and items directly from the interaction graph, rather than from handcrafted features, yields richer collaborative signals for recommendation tasks [S2:c5f5f179d80a3bf9b4f29750283a87eaca42e91b].

Building on the graph formulation, later studies refined the graph topology and propagation mechanisms.  Star‑GNN introduced a star‑shaped graph that aggregates item information through a central hub, reducing the number of propagation steps while preserving global session context [S2:63f9bc0d97bdfc80b0227415d170941c211acf43].  Recognizing that pairwise edges ignore higher‑order item co‑occurrences, Self‑Supervised Hypergraph Convolutional Networks modeled sessions as hypergraphs, enabling the capture of beyond‑pairwise relations among items [S2:c3ef11a7a8a46f1f193250dd68838cb72b7de0bc].  Global Context Enhanced GNN further extended the scope of graph construction by incorporating item transitions from all historical sessions, allowing the model to leverage cross‑session information while attenuating irrelevant noise [S2:b05a5424d0fce45896b6b8a847cf540a38f556bc].

Temporal dynamics and inter‑session collaboration have also been incorporated into graph‑based SBR.  Temporal Augmented GNN added time‑aware edges and temporal encoding to the session graph, explicitly modeling interest drift over long time spans and improving next‑item prediction in evolving environments [S2:dc3874003319001f276ec752dd427ac338619bf4].  Collaborative Graph Learning argued that supervision derived only from intra‑session sequences is insufficient, and introduced auxiliary inter‑session graph signals that jointly supervise item representation learning, leading to more robust embeddings [S2:0552e5f53bb30cda3e838e7e136490790a6527f8].  Moreover, a multi‑behavior GNN framework extended the graph to encode heterogeneous interaction types (e.g., clicks, likes, purchases), enriching the session representation with richer behavioral cues [S2:3a0b49179ce8f3ed5fe0d104f7c3817f7449770c].

The most recent trend exploits self‑supervised learning to alleviate the severe data sparsity inherent in SBR.  Self‑Supervised Graph Co‑Training proposes a dual‑GNN architecture that generates pseudo‑labels through mutual information maximization and contrastive learning, thereby providing additional training signals without external annotations [S2:3dc2abdc8cad9841a570e9edefb717ed11510b0f].
